title: Life at Sagamore Hill
subtitle: The Roosevelts at Home
intro: Six children, a formidable wife who ran the household and the president, a menagerie of pets, and a hill above Oyster Bay that stayed home for thirty-four years. Fifteen questions on the Roosevelts off duty.

heroCredit: Theodore and Edith Roosevelt with Alice, Ted, Kermit, Ethel and the infant Archie, photographed by C. M. Gilbert, January 1895 — five children; Quentin, the sixth, was born two years later. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

tiers.line: Perfect. Even Edith would be impressed.

tiers.name: Eldest Child
tiers.line: You know where everything is kept.

tiers.name: Lost on the Drive

questions.prompt: How many children did Theodore Roosevelt have?
questions.explanation: Six: Alice, from his first marriage, and then Ted Jr., Kermit, Ethel, Archie and Quentin with Edith. Contemporaries noted that the White House had not seen anything like them.
questions.imageAlt: Theodore and Edith Roosevelt seated with five children in a studio group portrait, the youngest a baby
questions.credit: Theodore and Edith Roosevelt with Alice, Ted, Kermit, Ethel and the infant Archie, photographed by C. M. Gilbert, January 1895 — five children; Quentin, the sixth, was born two years later. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.explanation: Edith Kermit Carow. They married in London in December 1886, and from then on she ran Sagamore Hill — the accounts, the farm, the staff, the children, and most days the president himself. Her word on the house was final, and nobody, her husband included, argued with it for long.
questions.imageAlt: Théobald Chartran's painted portrait of Edith Kermit Roosevelt in a plumed hat, seated on a stone bench in a garden
questions.credit: Théobald Chartran's 1902 portrait of Edith Kermit Roosevelt, photographed by Frances Benjamin Johnston. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: What was the Roosevelt home at Oyster Bay called?
questions.explanation: Sagamore Hill, named for the Sagamore Mohannis, a chief who had signed away rights to the land generations earlier. Roosevelt built it in 1884–85 and it was home until he died there in 1919.
questions.credit: The Parlor, Sagamore Hill. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: Roosevelt's eldest daughter Alice was famous in her own right. For what?
options: Her landscape painting and gallery shows
Her volunteer nursing in France during the war
Her career on the New York stage
questions.explanation: She refused, publicly and consistently, to behave as a president's daughter was supposed to. She smoked in public, drove her own car, kept a green snake called Emily Spinach — named for a very thin aunt — and said whatever she liked to whomever she liked. Her father is supposed to have remarked that he could run the country or control Alice, but not both. It was her sister Ethel, not Alice, who went to the war: Ethel served as a Red Cross nurse in Paris.
questions.imageAlt: Theodore and Edith Roosevelt seated with five children in a studio group portrait, the youngest a baby
questions.credit: Theodore and Edith Roosevelt with Alice, Ted, Kermit, Ethel and the infant Archie, photographed by C. M. Gilbert, January 1895 — five children; Quentin, the sixth, was born two years later. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: Alice Roosevelt's 1906 White House wedding made her famous. Whom did she marry?
options: William Borah, the senator from Idaho
questions.explanation: Nicholas Longworth, an Ohio congressman who later became Speaker of the House. The wedding was a national event and the shade of blue in her gown became a fashion — “Alice blue.” They married in the East Room on February 17, 1906, and the newspapers gave it the front page. The colour outlasted the marriage, which was not a happy one, and a hit song kept it in circulation for another generation.
questions.imageAlt: Theodore and Edith Roosevelt seated with five children in a studio group portrait, the youngest a baby
questions.credit: Theodore and Edith Roosevelt with Alice, Ted, Kermit, Ethel and the infant Archie, photographed by C. M. Gilbert, January 1895 — five children; Quentin, the sixth, was born two years later. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: What went on at Cooper's Bluff, a mile from Sagamore Hill?
options: Sunday services were held on the sand in fine weather
They raced one another down a huge sandbank into the bay
The children's schoolhouse stood at the foot of it
A gate lodge stood where the drive met the shore road
questions.explanation: Roosevelt called it “a gigantic sand-bank rising from the edge of the bay,” and the family ran handicap races down it, timed and started one after another. If the tide was high some of them were sure to run into the water, which was most of the appeal. His sister Corinne remembered as many as twenty children lined up on top waiting for the word go, and her brother turning to them with a twinkle in his eye: “There is a little path down the side, but I always jump off the top.”
questions.imageAlt: Ted, Archie and Ethel Roosevelt on a windy day at Sagamore Hill
questions.credit: Ted, Archie, and Ethel Roosevelt one windy day at Sagamore Hill, Oyster Bay. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: What was Edith Roosevelt's role in the 1902 White House renovation?
options: She opposed it as an extravagance
She insisted the family live elsewhere permanently
She left it entirely to the architects McKim, Mead & White
questions.explanation: She drove it, and what she wanted out of it was the working offices pushed clear of the family's living quarters — the arrangement that produced what everyone now calls the West Wing. Charles McKim gutted the building to do it, and the Roosevelts lived elsewhere for six months while he worked. She also established the White House china collection and the practice of a first lady employing a social secretary.
questions.imageAlt: Théobald Chartran's painted portrait of Edith Kermit Roosevelt in a plumed hat, seated on a stone bench in a garden
questions.credit: Théobald Chartran's 1902 portrait of Edith Kermit Roosevelt, photographed by Frances Benjamin Johnston. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: The Roosevelt children were notorious in Washington for what?
options: Being kept strictly out of the newspapers
Being sent abroad to school in England
Treating the White House as a playground
Their unfailingly formal manners in public
questions.explanation: They roamed it. Snakes, a badger, a macaw, guinea pigs, a one-legged rooster and a pony named Algonquin — who was famously taken up in the White House lift to visit Archie when he was ill. Quentin and his friends became known to the nation as the White House Gang, which tells you how far the reputation travelled. Staff described the place as under occupation.
questions.imageAlt: Ted, Archie and Ethel Roosevelt on a windy day at Sagamore Hill
questions.credit: Ted, Archie, and Ethel Roosevelt one windy day at Sagamore Hill, Oyster Bay. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: Which Roosevelt son died in the First World War?
questions.explanation: Quentin, the youngest, a pilot shot down over France in July 1918 at twenty. All four sons served; Archie and Ted were both wounded. Roosevelt had spent years preaching that the strenuous life meant risk, and the bill came due.
questions.imageAlt: Portrait of Mrs. Roosevelt with Quentin
questions.credit: Mrs. Roosevelt, Quentin. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: Ted Jr. distinguished himself in the Second World War. How?
options: He commanded a bomber group over Germany
He led the Marine landing on Iwo Jima
He planned the Doolittle raid on Tokyo
He landed at Utah Beach on D-Day
questions.explanation: Theodore Roosevelt Jr., aged fifty-six and walking with a cane, went ashore in the first wave at Utah Beach — the only general officer to land with a first wave anywhere that morning — and reorganised the assault when it came in off target. He received the Medal of Honor for it, and died of a heart attack in Normandy the following month, having never learned the award was coming.
questions.imageAlt: Ted, Archie and Ethel Roosevelt at Sagamore Hill
questions.credit: Ted, Archie, and Ethel Roosevelt one windy day at Sagamore Hill, Oyster Bay. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: Which son accompanied his father both to Africa and down the River of Doubt?
questions.explanation: Kermit, on both expeditions. In Brazil he refused to leave his father behind when Roosevelt, feverish and infected, urged the party to go on without him.
questions.imageAlt: Theodore and Edith Roosevelt seated with five children in a studio group portrait, the youngest a baby
questions.credit: Theodore and Edith Roosevelt with Alice, Ted, Kermit, Ethel and the infant Archie, photographed by C. M. Gilbert, January 1895 — five children; Quentin, the sixth, was born two years later. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: What did Roosevelt famously do with his children at Sagamore Hill and in Rock Creek Park?
options: Timed foot races round the meadow
Compass courses set the night before
questions.explanation: The rule was that you went in a straight line to the chosen point and took whatever lay between you and it — over the haystack, through the stream, up the cliff, never around. Diplomats invited along tended to arrive back soaked. The French ambassador Jules Jusserand famously kept up, and the story that made his name in Washington is that he swam Rock Creek without taking his gloves off, on the grounds that they might meet ladies.
questions.imageAlt: Ted, Archie and Ethel Roosevelt at Sagamore Hill
questions.credit: Ted, Archie, and Ethel Roosevelt one windy day at Sagamore Hill, Oyster Bay. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: What did Roosevelt often send his younger children when he was away?
questions.explanation: Letters full of pen-and-ink drawings of animals, boats and jokes. A selection was published after his death as Theodore Roosevelt's Letters to His Children, and it did more for his popular reputation than most of his political writing. The drawings are not good, exactly, but they are unmistakably his, and they were sent from wherever he happened to be — the White House, a train, a tent in East Africa.
questions.credit: Library at Sagamore Hill. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.explanation: In Youngs Memorial Cemetery at Oyster Bay, a short distance from Sagamore Hill, on a wooded slope. Edith is buried beside him. There was no state funeral — the arrangements were deliberately plain.
questions.credit: The Parlor, Sagamore Hill. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: How long did Edith Roosevelt outlive her husband?
questions.explanation: She died in 1948, twenty-nine years after him, having lived to see Ted Jr. killed in Normandy and Kermit dead in Alaska. She burned much of her own correspondence, which is why she remains the least knowable figure in the family — and she kept Sagamore Hill going for most of those thirty years, largely out of the public eye.
